youtube.baslik: Language Milestones from Birth to Age Five | Lesson 75 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In this lesson we look at the milestones of language development from birth to age five: cooing and canonical babbling, first words and two-word combinations, and preschool language skills. We also discuss how babbling relates to hearing, the warning signs, and language assessment tools used in Türkiye.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: ASHA, Communication Milestones; Oller DK, Eilers RE (1988), The role of audition in infant babbling, Child Development; Aksu-Koç A, Slobin DI (1985), The acquisition of Turkish, The Crosslinguistic Study of Language Acquisition; Topbaş S, Güven S (2011), Türkçe Erken Dil Gelişimi Testi (TEDİL).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Cooing, babbling and first words from birth to age five
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the milestones of language development from birth to age five.
We will follow the path from cooing and babbling to first words and sentences, with the warning signs an audiologist should know.
When we talk about language development, we separate two main areas.
Receptive language is the child's ability to understand what is said to them.
Expressive language is the child's ability to convey thoughts with words and sentences.
Children usually understand much more than they can say; receptive language runs ahead of expressive language.
Speech is the production of language with sounds; a child may have good language but trouble with speech sounds, or the reverse.
Hearing is the input on which all these skills are built.
Milestones are given as an age range rather than a single age, because development varies from child to child.
Milestones show skills most children gain in that range; ASHA stresses that they are not screening or diagnostic tools.
So a child gaining a skill a little late does not, by itself, mean there is a problem.
For babies born preterm, assessment is based on corrected age, especially in the first years.
However, delays in more than one area, or expected skills that never appear, must always be assessed.
For children who hear more than one language, vocabulary is assessed by counting the words in both languages together.
In the first three months, the baby reacts to sounds and calms down or smiles when spoken to.
In this period, the baby makes soft, vowel-like sounds; this is called cooing.
Between four and six months, the baby laughs, reacts to toys that make sounds and plays with sounds.
At about six to ten months, regular repeated syllables such as ba-ba-ba begin; this is called canonical babbling.
At seven to nine months, the baby looks when called by name; at ten to twelve months, waves, points and understands simple words.
In this period, gestures such as pointing and waving are important forerunners of spoken language.
First meaningful words appear at around twelve months.
Cooing consists of soft, vowel-like sounds coming from the throat.
Over time, the baby starts to use the lips and tongue to play with sound.
In canonical babbling, the baby combines a consonant and a vowel to produce regular syllables such as ba-ba or da-da.
Then variegated babbling begins, in which different syllables follow each other, such as ba-da-gu.
Toward the end of the first year, some babies produce long strings of sound with the melody of speech but no words; this is called jargon.
Babbling is an important exercise in which the baby matches the sounds of the language they hear with their own voice.
Babies with severe hearing loss can also coo, so cooing is not taken as evidence of hearing.
Canonical babbling, however, depends largely on the baby hearing language and their own voice.

cumleler.yazi: In the nineteen eighty eight study by Oller and Eilers, all hearing babies began canonical babbling by ten months at the latest.

cumleler: In babies with severe and profound loss, canonical babbling began after eleven months, sometimes much later.
This finding shows that late onset of babbling may be an early sign of hearing loss.
In a baby who is ten to eleven months old and does not produce regular syllables, hearing must always be assessed.
First words usually appear at around twelve months and relate to family members, food and toys.
In this period, a child can express a whole request with one word; for example, water can mean I want water.
Vocabulary grows slowly at first; in many children, learning speeds up clearly after a certain point.
According to ASHA, between nineteen and twenty four months most children understand and use at least fifty different words.
In the same period, two-word combinations such as mommy come or give ball begin.
The child begins to understand simple instructions such as bring the ball, even without gestures.
In this period, speech is not yet fully intelligible; words may be said in simplified forms.

maddeler.metin: Suffixes are _at risk_ in high-frequency loss

cumleler: Turkish is an agglutinative language; meaning is carried by suffixes added to the word root.
Studies of Turkish acquisition report that children begin to use noun and verb suffixes during the first word combinations.
So even in the two-word stage, Turkish children may use suffixed forms such as topu, the ball, and anneye, to mommy.
In Turkish, word order in the sentence is relatively flexible; meaning is largely set by the suffixes.
So a child who misses suffixes may also miss the information on who did what to whom in the sentence.
For this reason, language assessment in Turkish-speaking children looks not only at vocabulary size but also at suffix use.
Between two and three years, sentences get longer and the child forms sentences of two or three words.
The child asks questions such as what and where, and says their name when asked.
Between three and four years, the child begins to tell about an event they lived through or a story from a book.
In this period, more complex sentences joined with conjunctions appear, and tense suffixes become more varied.
According to ASHA, between four and five years most children recognize ten or more letters and begin to write their name.
Around age four, speech usually becomes intelligible to unfamiliar people as well.
Some difficult sounds, such as r, may continue to develop until later.
In the preschool years, the child becomes able to tell an event with a beginning, middle and end.
Phonological awareness skills such as finding rhymes and counting syllables develop; these are the building blocks of reading.
Why and how questions become frequent; the child also uses language to learn.
The child learns to take turns in conversation, stay on topic and adjust their speech to the listener.
These skills show why hearing matters not only for hearing speech but also for success at school.
Some findings are warning signs showing that the child must be assessed.
One of them is a twelve-month-old baby who does not babble, point or wave.
A sixteen-month-old child who uses no single words at all should also be assessed.
A twenty four-month-old child who does not form two-word phrases spontaneously is another warning sign.
At any age, the loss of language or social skills already gained calls for urgent assessment.
In every child with a speech or language delay, hearing must always be assessed, even if another cause is suspected.

ogeler.metin: Language test given to the child

cumleler: In Türkiye, there are standardized tools adapted to Turkish for assessing language development.

cumleler.yazi: The Turkish Communicative Development Inventory, TİGE, is the parent-report Turkish adaptation of the MacArthur-Bates inventory.
cumleler.ses: The Turkish Communicative Development Inventory, Tee-geh, is the parent-report Turkish adaptation of the MacArthur-Bates inventory.

cumleler.yazi: The Turkish Test of Early Language Development, TEDİL, adapted from the TELD-3 by Topbaş and Güven, is given directly to the child.
cumleler.ses: The Turkish Test of Early Language Development, Tedil, adapted from the T.E.L.D. three by Topbash and Guven, is given directly to the child.

cumleler: Giving and interpreting these tests is the speech-language therapist's field; the audiologist refers when needed and shares hearing data.
In a child with hearing loss, the results of language assessment also guide hearing aid fitting and the intervention plan.

sahneler.metin: In the case history, ask concrete questions: when did the child babble, say a first word, how many words now? If delayed, assess hearing in detail.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: in a child's case history, ask concrete questions instead of general ones such as how is their speech.
When did the child babble, when did they say their first word, how many words do they use now, do they combine two words?
Compare the family's answers with the milestones and write any possible delay in the report.
If there is a delay, examine hearing in detail with age-appropriate methods, together with a middle ear assessment.
Children understand more than they can say; receptive language runs ahead of expressive language.
Cooing starts in the first months and canonical babbling at about six to ten months; late babbling may point to hearing loss.
First words appear at about twelve months, and two-word combinations between eighteen and twenty four months.
In every child with a language delay, hearing must always be assessed.

sahneler.soru: Which finding is a stronger sign of hearing loss?
sahneler.aciklama: Babies with severe loss can also _coo_; canonical babbling depends on hearing and is delayed with hearing loss.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in an eleven-month-old baby, which finding is a stronger sign of hearing loss?
The correct answer is B: delayed canonical babbling.

cumleler: Cooing can also be seen in babies with severe loss, while regular repeated syllables depend largely on hearing.
